title: Async/Await & Cooperative Concurrency
summary: Single-threaded concurrency via an event loop — how async/await sugars futures and promises into linear-looking code, why it's brilliant for I/O and useless for CPU work, and how one blocking call can freeze an entire server.

slides.markdown:
`threads-and-the-shared-memory-model` ended on a question: if shared mutable state is the problem, what do you do instead? Async/await's answer is unusual — it doesn't remove sharing, it removes the *threads*.

**Async/await** gives you one thread, handling many in-flight operations at once, switching between them cooperatively at specific points (`await`) instead of the OS preempting threads whenever it likes. No two pieces of *your* code ever run at literally the same instant, which sidesteps an entire category of races by construction — not by discipline, and not by removing shared state, but by removing the possibility of two threads touching it simultaneously.

This is the dominant concurrency model for I/O-heavy servers — Node.js, modern Python (`asyncio`), C#'s `async`/`await`, and Rust's `async` all use variations of this idea.

slides.subTitle: One thread, cooperative switching
slides.markdown:
The mental model: one thread runs a queue of tasks, and each task runs uninterrupted *until it hits an await point* — a place where it's waiting on something external (a network response, a timer, a file read). At that point, the task voluntarily yields control back to the **event loop**, which picks up whichever other task is ready to make progress next.

This is **cooperative** scheduling: a task decides when to yield (at an `await`), unlike OS thread preemption, which can interrupt a thread at any instruction. The upside is real: no two tasks ever execute simultaneously, so there's no need for locks protecting your own in-process state from concurrent access — only one task is ever "live" at a time. The downside is exactly as direct: a task that never yields (a long CPU-bound loop with no `await`) blocks everything else on that thread until it finishes.

slides.subTitle: A value that isn't ready yet
slides.markdown:
A **future** (or **promise** in JavaScript) is a value representing "the result of an operation that hasn't completed yet." It starts in a pending state, and eventually resolves to either a success value or an error — code can attach callbacks to run once that resolution happens, without blocking the current thread waiting for it.

This is the mechanism underneath async/await, not a separate concept: an `await someAsyncCall()` is, underneath, attaching "resume this function from here" as a callback on the future/promise `someAsyncCall()` returns, then yielding control back to the event loop until that callback fires. Async/await is a *syntax* layer over futures/promises — the runtime capability is the same either way.

`async`/`await` is genuinely just sugar — the compiler transforms your linear-looking code into a **state machine** (or, in some implementations, a chain of continuations) behind the scenes. Each `await` becomes a point where the generated state machine can suspend, remembering exactly where it was (local variables and all), and resume later when the awaited value is ready.

This is why async functions can be written to *look* like ordinary sequential code — `const result = await fetchData(); process(result);` — while the compiler is actually generating the callback-registration and control-flow logic a hand-written promise chain would need spelled out explicitly. Knowing this desugaring is what lets you correctly reason about where execution actually pauses, rather than just where the code visually appears to "wait."

slides.sectionTitle: Why async shines for I/O and does nothing for CPU
slides.markdown:
Async/await's entire performance win comes from overlapping **wait time**, not computation. While one task is awaiting a network response — time the CPU would otherwise spend idle — the event loop runs a different task's code. Ten thousand tasks each waiting 100ms on a database call can all be "in flight" on one thread, because none of them are using the CPU while they wait.

A CPU-bound task breaks this completely: it never hits an `await`, so it never yields, and it occupies the single event-loop thread computing for its entire duration — nothing else on that thread makes progress meanwhile. This connects directly to `threads-and-the-shared-memory-model`'s concurrency-vs-parallelism distinction: async/await buys concurrency (many tasks in flight) with zero parallelism (only one ever executing), which is exactly the right trade for I/O-bound work and exactly the wrong tool for CPU-bound work.

The single most common async/await production incident: a synchronous, blocking call slipped into async code — a synchronous file read, a CPU-heavy JSON parse of a huge payload, a call into a library that doesn't itself support async and blocks the calling thread.

Because the whole model relies on the current task voluntarily yielding at an `await`, a call that blocks *without* yielding doesn't just slow down its own task — it freezes the entire event loop, and every other in-flight request on that thread, for the duration of the block. This is precisely why "why does one slow synchronous call in this async handler freeze all other requests?" is such a common debugging question: the answer is always the same shape — something in that handler isn't actually yielding control, whether or not it *looks* asynchronous on the surface.

The fix is finding and either replacing the blocking call with a genuinely async equivalent, or (for unavoidable CPU-heavy work) offloading it to a worker thread/process pool so it doesn't occupy the event-loop thread at all.

| | Node.js | Python `asyncio` |
|---|---|---|
| Default execution model | Single-threaded event loop by default | Single-threaded event loop by default |
| CPU-bound escape hatch | Worker threads (`worker_threads`), or child processes | `multiprocessing`, or `run_in_executor` for a thread/process pool |
| Why single-threaded at all | Design choice, simplicity — no GIL-style constraint forcing it | CPython's GIL (`dynamic-language-runtimes-v8-and-cpython`) makes true multi-threaded CPU parallelism unavailable anyway, so async fits naturally |

The two ecosystems converge on the same model for related but distinct reasons: Node.js chose single-threaded-by-default deliberately; CPython's GIL means multi-threading wouldn't have bought CPU parallelism anyway, so `asyncio`'s concurrency-without-parallelism model isn't giving up much that threading would have offered for I/O-bound work in the first place.

Async/await solves the shared-memory problem by removing true concurrent execution of your own code, but it introduces its own failure modes — a fire-and-forget promise that nobody awaits, a task that outlives the request that spawned it — which is exactly what `structured-concurrency` exists to discipline, regardless of whether the underlying model is async/await, threads, or actors.

`comparing-concurrency-models` puts async/await side by side with threads, actors, and CSP against the same "handle 10,000 concurrent connections" problem, making the trade-offs from this topic and the last one concrete and comparable.
